author: Claude (EFL materials writer role), v2 against the quality gate
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate and the grammatical-range check. The workbook text failed on every measure: sentence length and lexical load sat below band at A2 and B1, the B2 reached its difficulty through C1/C2 vocabulary while its syntax stayed B1, and A2 and B1 overlapped at 0.42 - the per-slide ceiling - so the three levels were re-conceived as separate texts rather than paraphrases of one another. Every fact, name and number of the source is kept (2030 on slide 19 is the mission's only number). Facts corrected, with the reason: slide 2, 'empirical evidence proves that gender equity is an economic necessity' and 'true global progress remains impossible when half of the world's population is marginalized' overstate what the research shows, so the claim is now that the evidence links women's progress to stronger households, better schools and faster growth, and that progress stays slow while half a population is held back; slide 7, the source asserts as a blanket fact that women are paid less 'for identical responsibilities', which conflates the raw gap with the same-job gap, corrected to what the data support - women earn less on average and a measurable gap survives after economists control for occupation, hours and experience; slide 12, 'remaining neutral is equivalent to compliance' is both the wrong word (complicity) and a slogan asserting more than the source supports, replaced by the concrete consequence that silence leaves the person isolated; slide 14, 'marginalized women in isolated communities acquire advanced degrees' overstates remote learning, reduced to following a whole course on a borrowed tablet; slide 16, 'gender equity directly correlates with robust macroeconomic stability' hedged to participation tending to raise national output; slide 5, 'stifles cognitive diversity' reduced to narrowing what a child can imagine; slide 10, evaluation 'solely on merit' de-absolutised; slide 19, 'we can make a fair world by 2030' reframed as the deadline the goals name and how much closer this generation can pull it, since no country has yet reached parity; slide 20, the workbook's closing 'Thank you very much' removed under the house rule that the speech ends on the claim, and the B2's 'Let us examine/exit/accept' changed to 'let's'. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count. A2 keeps one clause per sentence, present and past simple and no participle clauses, and carries the argument in concrete everyday words.

slides.1: Hello everyone. Today let's look at SDG 5, the goal for gender equality. It means that boys and girls get the same rights and the same dreams.
slides.2: Why does this matter to you and to me? Equality is not only a women's story. When girls do well, our homes get stronger and our schools get better.
slides.3: Imagine a bird for a moment. A bird only needs two wings to fly. Our world needs two wings as well, so men and women must carry it together.
slides.4: In the past, many people said that boys become doctors and girls stay at home. Those old ideas are like walls. They stop children from following their dreams.
slides.5: This starts when we are very young. Adults give trucks to boys and dolls to girls. Those presents teach children what to want, so let's open every toy box.
slides.6: In some poor countries, girls leave school early. Many never learn to read or write. Then good jobs stay closed, and their children begin in the same place.
slides.7: Now look at pay. Women still earn less than men on average, and some of that difference stays inside the same job. Equal work deserves equal pay.
slides.8: Now count the bosses. Most big companies and governments are still led by men. Women have strong ideas, and we need them in the room where choices happen.
slides.9: Look at the unpaid work at home. Women usually do the cleaning, the cooking and the childcare, and nobody pays for it. Men and boys must take a share.
slides.10: So how do we start? Respect comes first. Listen to your classmates with real attention, and never say that a job belongs to boys or to girls.
slides.11: Take it home with you. Boys can cook the dinner, and girls can fix the bike. When everybody helps, the housework shrinks and the family grows closer.
slides.12: Now think about school. If someone is treated badly because she is a girl, then say something. One brave voice in the classroom can change a whole year.
slides.13: Here is the good news. More girls now build robots and write computer code. STEM is open to everybody, and these girls will be our next engineers.
slides.14: The internet also opens doors. In far villages, a girl can watch a school lesson on a cheap computer. The old school walls are much thinner than before.
slides.15: Open your phone tonight. You will find athletes, artists and leaders who are women. Their stories reach millions of young people, so please pass them on.
slides.16: Laws are changing too. More countries now promise fair pay and safe work for women. When women can work freely, the whole country often grows richer.
slides.17: Let's look back. We saw old problems, and we also saw new ideas. Gender equality is not a dream — it is a real goal for schools, work and family.
slides.18: Here is my promise: I will treat every classmate the same, whatever their gender. What about you? Wash the dishes tonight, or cheer up a friend.
slides.19: Big change needs time and patience. The goals give the world only one deadline, and it is 2030. Let's be the people who move us really close.
slides.20: SDG 5 is a mission for you and for me. When women and men stand together as equals, every family grows stronger. That is the world I really want.
